n: Job is tired of living, so he will let his complaint flow freely and speak from his bitterness. This whole chapter is addressed to God — raw, honest prayer.

f.w: I will leave my complaint upon myself
f.g: I will give free rein to my complaint.

f.w: My soul is weary of my life

n: He asks God not to simply condemn him, but to show him the charges. Job wants to know why he is suffering.

f.w: shew me wherefore thou contendest with me
f.g: Tell me what charge you have against me.

n: Does it please you, God, to crush the work of your own hands while smiling on the plans of the wicked? Job appeals to God as his Creator.
Do you see with human eyes, limited and easily fooled? Job knows God sees perfectly — so why treat him as a suspect?
Is your life short like a human’s, so you must rush to find fault before time runs out?
Why then do you search so hard for my sin?
You know I’m not guilty, yet no one can rescue me from your power. Job is confident in his innocence but feels trapped.

f.w: Thou knowest that I am not wicked

n: Your hands shaped me with care — and now you would destroy me? It doesn’t make sense to Job that a loving Creator would ruin His own work.
Remember that you made me from clay. Will you now turn me back to dust?
Job describes his formation in the womb in poetic language: like milk poured out and thickened into cheese.

f.g: An ancient image of how a body takes shape in the womb.

n: God clothed him with skin and flesh and knit him together with bones and sinews. Compare the wonder of Psalm 139.

f.w: fenced me with bones and sinews
f.g: Wove me together with bones and tendons.

f.w: clothed me with skin and flesh

n: You gave me life and showed me steadfast love, and your care watched over my spirit. Job remembers God’s past goodness.
But now Job suspects God had a hidden purpose all along — to watch for his faults. In a deeper sense, God did have a hidden purpose, as the reader knows from chapters 1–2.
If I sin, you watch me and won’t forgive me.
If I’m guilty, I’m doomed; if I’m innocent, I still can’t lift my head in honor. I am filled with shame — look at my misery.

f.w: yet will I not lift up my head
f.g: I can’t hold my head up — I’m covered in shame.

n: If I lift my head, you hunt me like a lion and again show your awesome power against me.

f.w: Thou huntest me as a fierce lion

n: You keep bringing new witnesses against me and increase your anger; wave after wave of troubles attacks me.

f.g: Perhaps his sores and losses, which seem to “testify” against him.
Wave after wave of attacking forces.

n: Why did you let me be born? I wish I had died before anyone saw me. Job returns to the lament of chapter 3.

f.w: Wherefore then hast thou brought me forth out of the womb?

n: It would have been better never to have existed — carried straight from the womb to the grave.
My life is short; just leave me alone so I can have a little comfort.

f.g: Brighten up a little; find a moment of cheer.

n: ...before I go to the place from which I won’t return — the land of darkness and deep shadow.
Job pictures the realm of the dead as a land of gloom and chaos, where even the light is dark. He has not yet seen the fuller light that later revelation brings about life after death.

f.w: where the light is as darkness
